subject: Critical Thinking
title: Everyday Logic: Spotting Bad Arguments at Work
description: A 60-second lesson on Everyday Logic: Spotting Bad Arguments at Work.

hook.text: 'We've always done it this way.' That's not an argument — it's a refusal to think. And it's everywhere.

buildup.text: Workplaces run on informal logic: proposals, justifications, cost-benefit claims, risk assessments.

discovery.text: Most bad business decisions come from hidden assumptions nobody questioned, not from bad data.

twist.text: The most powerful question in any meeting: 'What would have to be true for this to be wrong?'

climax.text: Asking for evidence, checking assumptions, and naming trade-offs — that's logic without formulas.

punchline.text: You don't need symbols. You need the habit of asking 'why?'

quiz.question: What is the most common source of bad business decisions?

details.summary: Everyday logic applies formal reasoning principles to the arguments encountered in workplaces, media, and personal conversations. Spotting bad arguments in real time requires recognizing common patterns of flawed reasoning.
details.whyItMatters: Most bad reasoning encountered in life is not in textbooks but in meetings, ads, and conversations where quick evaluation skills matter most.
takeaways: Most workplace arguments contain informal fallacies
Recognizing patterns is faster than formal analysis
Asking 'does the conclusion follow from the premises?' is the key habit

faq.question: What is the most useful logical skill for everyday professional life?
faq.answer: The habit of separating claims from evidence and asking whether the evidence actually supports the conclusion. Most bad arguments fail this basic test.

faq.question: How can you politely call out a bad argument in a meeting?
faq.answer: Ask clarifying questions: 'What evidence supports that conclusion?' or 'Are there other explanations?' This exposes flaws without directly attacking the speaker.
